paras: The lynching of Jim McMillan was the killing of a Black man by a mob of white men near Green Pond, Alabama, in mid-June 1919, during a search for a man accused of an attempted assault on a white woman. The same mob drove George Lightsey, a Black landowner, from his home, and four white men were jailed on a charge of being members of the party that shot McMillan.

According to the Chicago Defender, the trouble began with an alleged attempted assault on a white woman about 2 o'clock on a Monday afternoon, about two miles from Lightsey's home and across the line in Bibb County. Lightsey lived at Green Pond in Tuscaloosa County, where he owned 21 1/2 acres of farm land and eight tenant houses.

Between 12 and 1 o'clock the following Tuesday morning, a mob surrounded Lightsey's house, tried to raise the windows near which he slept, and ordered him to come out under threat of death. Lightsey ran out the back door and down a lane and hid in the swamps about three miles away. The mob then took his brother from bed, made him lead a search for Lightsey, and threatened to "batter her damn brains out" when Lightsey's wife pleaded with them.

"Bent on putting some one to death," in the Defender's words, the mob went next to the home of Jim McMillan. According to Mrs. Lightsey, the men put on him a pair of blue overalls and a white shirt like those the woman said her attacker had worn, and carried him before her to be identified. The woman was said to have fired the first shot, which struck him in the mouth, after which the mob put him to death.

A Centerville dispatch dated June 20 reported that four white men, charged with being members of the party, had been jailed at midnight Thursday and that a special jury of the Bibb County court had been summoned for June 23 to investigate. The Ohio State Monitor named the jailed men as J. Blackenship, James D. Oglesby, Elisha Green and Tom Russell. The Defender also understood that several mob members were jailed "not for their murderous conduct, but for destruction of property belonging to the T. C. L. Co."

Lightsey said that when he tried to swear out warrants against members of the mob, most of whom he had known for years, he was refused and told they would look after it themselves. On a Friday morning he told his story to thirteen members of the Birmingham branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, accompanied by Frances Clinton, McMillan's sister-in-law. No report of the special jury's findings, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage.

The first report in the Black press was the Centerville wire item, which the Richmond Planet printed on June 28 as "Party of White Men Put Colored Man on Stump and Then Shoot Him," calling it an "alleged murder" and not naming the victim. The Ohio State Monitor ran the same dispatch on July 5 as "Four White Men Arrested for Lynching Negro," naming the accused, and repeated it on July 12.

The Baltimore Afro-American on July 4 and the Chicago Defender on July 5 instead told the story from Lightsey's side, naming McMillan. The Afro-American's headlines, "Wanted Two, But Only Got One" and "Alabama Mob Tries Hard For Double Lynching," presented Lightsey's escape and McMillan's death as one failed double lynching. The Defender gave the account at length under "Mob Forces Woman to Identify Man" and "Mob Killed McMillan," called it "the brutal murder," and noted that mob members were jailed for property damage rather than for the killing.

The accounts differ on how McMillan died: the Defender, relying on Mrs. Lightsey and on what "it is said," had the woman fire the first shot before the mob killed him, while the wire said the party forced him to stand on a stump and shot him. The Centerville report names no victim, but its location near Green Pond and its four arrests match the Defender's note that four mob members were held for McMillan's murder.

reader.title: Lynching of Jim McMillan
bases: A party of white men seized a Black man accused of an attack on a white woman and shot him to death, and four were jailed on a charge of being members of the party (A1, A5, A7).

McMillan was killed by a mob that had been hunting the man accused of an attempted assault on a white woman, and four white men were jailed as members of the party that shot him (A4, A5, A6, A7); no lawful authority is reported.

The Chicago Defender's account from George Lightsey (A4, A5, A6) and the separate Centerville wire (A1, A7) agree on a mob killing of a Black man near Green Pond and four arrests, though the wire names no victim and the two differ on details.

accounts.label: George Lightsey and Mrs. Lightsey (Black witnesses)
accounts.gist: A mob hunting the alleged assailant besieged Lightsey's house, drove him into the swamps, then dressed McMillan in clothes like the assailant's and brought him before the woman, who shot him; the mob finished killing him, and county officials refused warrants.

accounts.label: Centerville wire report
accounts.gist: A party of white men seized a Negro near Green Pond, forced him to stand on a stump and shot him to death; four white men were jailed and a special Bibb County jury summoned; other Negroes were maltreated and there had been racial trouble at Woodstock.

framing.detail: The Chicago Defender ran Lightsey's account under 'Mob Forces Woman to Identify Man' and 'Mob Killed McMillan', calling it 'the brutal murder' and noting mob members were jailed 'not for their murderous conduct' but for property damage.
The Baltimore Afro-American headlined 'Wanted Two, But Only Got One' and 'Alabama Mob Tries Hard For Double Lynching'.

The Richmond Planet and Ohio State Monitor ran the Centerville wire, the Planet under 'Party of White Men Put Colored Man on Stump and Then Shoot Him', the Monitor under 'Four White Men Arrested for Lynching Negro'.

versions.value: Arrests at midnight Thursday, in a dispatch dated June 20, 1919 (killing therefore before about June 19).
Mob raid early Tuesday morning after a Monday attack, in stories datelined July 4 and printed July 4-5, with no date of month.

conflicts.note: The two fit if the Tuesday was June 17; the Defender's 'latest dispatch' on four men held matches the wire's arrests. The record's July 1 is not supported.

versions.value: Bibb County (alleged attack across the line; men held and investigated by the Bibb County court at Centerville).

conflicts.note: Neither source states in which county McMillan was killed.

versions.value: The woman fired the first shot, into his mouth, and the mob then put him to death.
The party forced him to stand on a stump, where he was shot to death.

conflicts.note: The details differ but do not exclude each other; the Defender's version comes from Mrs. Lightsey and hearsay ('it is said').

record_check.dossier: About 1919-06-17 (inferred): a June 20 Centerville dispatch reports the arrests the previous Thursday, and the Defender places the raid early on a Tuesday.
Near Green Pond, Alabama; 'Tuscanica' is only the Afro-American's garbled dateline (the Defender datelines Tuscaloosa).
Contested: Green Pond in Tuscaloosa County per the Defender; alleged attack and court proceedings in Bibb County.
White men; four jailed and named: J. Blackenship, James D. Oglesby, Elisha Green, Tom Russell.
Also carried by the Richmond Planet (1919-06-28) and Ohio State Monitor (1919-07-05, 07-12).

info: Mob raid between 12 and 1 a.m. on a Tuesday after an alleged Monday-afternoon attack; the Centerville dispatch dated June 20 reports the four arrests at midnight Thursday, which places the killing about June 17, 1919 (inferred).
Near Green Pond, Alabama; Lightsey lived at Green Pond; the alleged attack was about two miles away across the line in Bibb County; the Afro-American datelined its story 'Tuscanica'.
Jim McMillan, killed; George Lightsey driven from his home; Lightsey's brother taken from bed; other Negroes in the section said to have been 'maltreated'.

An attempted criminal assault on a white woman on Monday afternoon by 'a light, brown-skinned man'; the woman was said to have been the victim of three attempted offenses (a Mexican who stole food, 'a big, black Negro' who stole clothing, and the assailant).
A mob of white men, several of them known to Lightsey for years; four jailed: J. Blackenship, James D. Oglesby, Elisha Green and Tom Russell.
No report of an indictment or trial was found.

quotes: after seizing a Negro forced him to stand on a stump, where he was shot to death, four white men were lodged in the county jail at midnight Thursday

'Wanted Two, But Only Got One': Lightsey fled to the woods, McMillan killed and buried; warrants refused. OCR garbled and condensed.
quotes: one colored man of this county was forced to take refuge in the woods, while another was put to death.
